Neonates of the Bynoe gecko (Heteronotia binoei 3N1B) emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs after an incubation period of roughly three months. At a constant incubation temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], hatching occurs at approximately 89 days [ab = approximately 89 days], a duration consistent with the prolonged developmental times observed in many gekkonid lizards at moderate temperatures. The hatchlings are notably diminutive, with a mean snout-to-vent length at birth of merely 2.14 centimeters [Lb = 2.14 centimeters]. Their corresponding wet weight at birth is minimal, computed to be approximately 0.22 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.22 grams] based on the length–mass scaling relationship derived from field-caught individuals. This combination of a prolonged incubation period and a small neonatal size reflects the energetic constraints of yolk-dependent embryogenesis within a cleidoic egg, a strategy typical of small-bodied, egg-laying reptiles inhabiting seasonally arid environments.

Sexual maturation in this parthenogenetic lineage is a gradual process that depends heavily on thermal opportunity. Under laboratory conditions maintained at a stable temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C], the time from hatching to the first reproduction event is approximately 212 days [tR = approximately 212 days], a figure derived from detailed growth records. This timeline represents about 123 days of post-hatching development added to the initial 89-day incubation period. The smallest female ever documented to have reproduced in the wild measured only 4.2 centimeters [Lp = 4.2 centimeters] in snout-to-vent length, a value that is likely an underestimate of the typical size at sexual maturation. The wet weight at puberty for a female of this length, as estimated from the species' length–weight relationship, is around 1.9 grams [Wwp = around 1.9 grams], indicating that reproductive investment begins when individuals have amassed a relatively modest body mass.

Adult body size in Heteronotia binoei 3N1B is exceptionally modest, even by the standards of its genus. The maximum or ultimate snout-to-vent length attained by this lineage reaches approximately 5.5 centimeters [Li = approximately 5.5 centimeters], a surprisingly small adult size for a gecko that can persist for many years. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for an individual of this length is roughly 4.6 grams [Wwi = roughly 4.6 grams], calculated from the same allometric equation used for earlier life stages. These values place the Bynoe gecko among the smallest of Australia's gekkonid lizards, a trait that may facilitate its occupation of cryptic microhabitats under exfoliating rock and in loose soil. Despite their minute dimensions, these geckos achieve relatively high population densities in the arid and semi-arid zones they inhabit, a testament to their efficient physiological design and low absolute resource demands.

The maximum reproductive rate of this unisexual species is surprisingly high given its small body size. Under favorable thermal conditions, specifically at a constant temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C], females have been observed to produce, on average, one egg clutch every 130 days [Ri = one egg clutch every 130 days], with each clutch containing a single egg [N_R_i = each clutch containing a single egg]. This translates to an annual reproductive output of roughly 2.8 eggs per year, a rate that is remarkably consistent across the active season when temperatures permit. The reproductive mode of obligate parthenogenesis means that every successfully incubated egg is a genetically identical daughter, allowing for rapid population growth from a single colonizing individual. This high intrinsic rate of increase is a key evolutionary advantage in the unpredictable and ephemeral habitats typical of Australia's interior.

The maximum lifespan of Heteronotia binoei 3N1B is notable for its duration, which far exceeds that of many similarly sized reptiles. At the relatively cool average environmental temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the species is estimated to have a maximum longevity of approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years], although this is almost certainly an underestimate. Captive records reported by Bauer suggest a minimum of 13.6 years, while the extraordinary field work of Kearney, Moritz, and Roberts documented the recapture of an individual at Paynes Find Station that had first been marked as an adult some 15 years earlier, implying a total lifespan potentially exceeding two decades. This extreme longevity, combined with a slow reproductive output per unit time, represents a classic bet-hedging strategy that buffers the population against repeated reproductive failures during prolonged droughts, ensuring that a cohort of experienced adult geckos persists through climatic perturbations.
